thread.title: FANGs Can Keep Growing Like Tech Stocks Even if They're Not Tech Stocks

title: FANGs Can Keep Growing Like Tech Stocks Even if They're Not Tech Stocks
text:
Illustration: courtesy of Google By Teresa Rivas Sept. 12, 2018 11:44 a.m. ET A reorganization of sectors means that many stocks that intuitively seem like tech technically won’t be. But the growth will remain, says Credit Suisse .
Where we were: A shrinking telecom sector spurred a major reorganization that will take place at the end of the month.
Where we’re headed: No matter what you call them, tech and Internet retail stocks look primed for more gains.
For many investors and consumers, tech is synonymous with the FANG stocks— Facebook (FB), Amazon.com (AMZN), Netflix (NFLX), and Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL). Yet fairly soon, none of those will be tech stocks, according to index providers.
As Barron’s first reported last fall , a new sector is in the works: Communications services will replace telecom and pull from other sectors as well, including technology. It’s a major, unprecedented move that will totally de-FANG the tech sector .
To be fair, tech already only had two FANGs, as Amazon and Netflix have been classified as consumer-discretionary stocks. But the further removal of Facebook and Google may make some investors wonder if the changes to the Global Industry Classification Standard, or GICS, system have addressed the disconnect between classifications and perception, or just shuffled the deck. (Although it will create opportunity for investors .)
No matter what you call them, however, the FANGs and other high-flying stocks aren’t likely to give up their monster growth any time soon. Credit Suisse ’s Jonathan Golub introduced last year a basket he calls TECH+, 25 tech and internet retail names covering industries from hardware to payment processors and semiconductor makers (with the FANGs, Apple [AAPL], and Microsoft [MSFT] high in the weightings). On Wednesday, he takes another look at TECH+, arguing it can continue to rally.
Since the 2009 market low, the basket has climbed 595%, Golub writes, compared to a 253% gain for the broader market, driven by revenue growth, rather than multiple-expansion, meaning that the stocks aren’t too richly valued despite their big runs. “Large addressable markets in Internet retail, online advertising, and cloud computing point to further upside,” he argues.
The TECH+ group is a “standout on revenue,” with projected 2019 sales growth estimated at 10.1%, above the projected 9.4% for the new communications services sector, the 5.4% expected for the remaining tech sector, and 5.3% for the S&P 500 overall. Moreover, amid a broadly stable margin environment for the wider market, TECH+ have been expanding their margins.
The stock’s “substantial” outperformance, driven by business success rather than valuation inflation, means that it’s “hard to make the case that TECH+ is problematically expensive,” Golub concludes.
Make the Connection
Saying sorry may not be enough for social media stocks.
Yet tech’s recent woes have been about more than just Facebook and Twitter (TWTR).
